>**In terms of the theoretical complexity, while the paper claims $O(1/K^2)$ result is achievable using first-order information, the analysis ends up relying on strong assumptions such as equation (10).**
Note that Equation (10) is intentionally not stated as an assumption; it is non-standard and serves mostly for illustrative purposes since it allows us to obtain the global $O(k^{-2})$ rate. However, it still motivates us to consider a much more interesting relaxation of the standard smoothness, Assumption 5.11, which covers the standard $L$-smoothness and allows us to establish the global $O(k^{-2})$ rate if $L_0=0$. This assumption is realistic since it holds for the separable logistic regression loss (Example 5.14).






>**In general, the first-order methods developed in the paper only guarantee an $O(1/K)$ convergence rate. I find the result relatively weak since it uses extra operations such as the Hessian vector product.**
That said, the case when $L_0=0$ occurs under a slightly different $L_0,L_1$ smoothness relaxation in the cutting-edge application [1]. In this case, a global $O(k^{-2})$ rate is proved by Corollary 5.15. Therefore, we view this as a significant direction for further study. Moreover, Hessian vector products (HVPs) are readily supported in modern frameworks (e.g., PyTorch) yet remain underutilized; with our experiments we show that exploring them has substantial potential. Further, CaCuAdGD is a non-accelerated method and it cannot be better than $O(k^{-1})$. Although accelerated methods enable faster rates, this should not stop studying non-accelerated methods. Moreover, while accelerated methods can achieve faster worst-case rates, this does not diminish the relevance of non-accelerated methods.For example, non-accelerated methods achieve linear convergence under strong convexity or the PL condition even without knowing the parameter, and they converge faster near minimisers. IKnown accelerated schemes  require an estimate of the strong-convexity parameter to guarantee linear convergence, whereas gradient descent does not. Our experiments also show that on well-conditioned problems accelerated variants can be slower (see Figures 23 and 24). Beyond rates, our contribution is conceptual: we identify a realistic regime – Assumption 5.11 with $L_0=0$ – under which a global $O(k^{-2})$ rate is provable, and we show that Hessian-vector products, which are readily supported in modern frameworks, can improve performance but remain underused. For these reasons, we do not view a non-accelerated $O(k^{-1})$ rate as a weak result; rather, it is a meaningful step that opens a promising line of research.
We would appreciate the opportunity to discuss these points further and address any remaining concerns.

>**Line 186, 254, 284 Gradient smoothness corresponds to Lipschitz Hessian; Hessian corresponds to the Lipschitzness of the third-order derivative.**
We believe there is a shift in terminology. Gradient $L$-smoothness means that the gradient is $L$-Lipschitz, which for twice-differentiable $f$ is implied by $\|\nabla^2 f(x)\|\le L$ on the relevant set. By contrast, “Lipschitz Hessian” is a stronger, third-order condition.
In Lines 186-189 we state that the standard smoothness (gradient $L$-smoothness) holds under Assumption 2.3 because the methods are monotone: the trajectory stays in the compact sublevel set $\mathcal L_0$, and since $f$ is twice differentiable, $L=\sup_{x\in\mathcal L_0}\|\nabla^2 f(x)\|<\infty$. This shows that a finite $L$ exists, even if it may be large. However, inequality (10) does not hold in general even on a compact set, so Line 254 is needed for the sake of rigor.
Assumption 5.11 (Line 356) relaxes standard smoothness: condition (14) holds with $L_0=\sup_{x\in\mathcal L_0}\|\nabla^2 f(x)\|$ and $L_1=0$, so the standard case is covered. See also Remark 5.12, which follows from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality:
$ \frac{\langle \nabla f(x), \nabla^2 f(x)\nabla f(x) \rangle}{\|\nabla f(x)\|^2} \le \frac{\|\nabla f(x)\|\,\|\nabla^2 f(x)\nabla f(x)\|}{\|\nabla f(x)\|^2} \le \|\nabla^2 f(x)\|,$ where $\|\nabla^2 f(x)\|$ is the maximum Hessian eigenvalue (assumed bounded under standard smoothness).
Assumption 5.11 is weaker because (a) it bounds only the directional second derivative and (b) it may hold with smaller constants; for example, Example 5.14 gives a real-world case with $L_0=0$. Since Assumption 5.11 is a relaxation, it is also automatically satisfied for some $(L_0,L_1)$ whenever standard smoothness holds.
We could not recognize any issue in Line 284; could the reviewer please specify?

> **I believe it's better to write down the final convergence rate (complexity), instead of leaving a recursive relation to the readers as in Theorem 6.3. Please be precise.**
>
>Our **claims are precise** and match Theorem 6.3. The theorem gives two per-iteration bounds that **each** yield an explicit rate **when that regime holds for all iterations**:
> - SGD-like regime ⇒ \(\|\nabla f(x^k)\|\) decreases as \(O(1/k)\).
> - cubic-Newton–like regime ⇒ \(\|\nabla f(x^k)\|\) decreases as \(O(1/k^{3/2})\).
> 
>In **mixed mode** (the method may switch regimes across iterations), a single telescoped complexity bound is nontrivial (discussed below Theorem 6.3) and, to our knowledge, open; we intentionally do **not** over-claim.
> 
> **Presentation edit.** We will add a short remark that states the two explicit rates when a single regime holds uniformly. This is a presentation edit, not a technical flaw, and **cannot justify rejection**.





>**I appreciate your honesty about the experiments. But it does not address my concerns: a new algorithm should be satisfy at least one of 1) practical efficiency; 2) strong theoretical performance, to be of interest. Given the current theoretical results, I still don't think the current results are satisfactory in terms of either of these two criteria.**
>  - Criterion (1): **practical efficiency.** On several hard benchmarks (e.g., covtype, w8a, ill-conditioned logsumexp) our method matches or exceeds strong non-accelerated adaptives (AdGD/Polyak) and often closes the gap to accelerated methods; HVPs are cheap in modern frameworks and can be replaced by vHv (computable with only forward passes). 
>
> - Criterion (2): **theory.** We recover the standard worst-case rate $O(1/k)$ for non-accelerated methods. We give a **new global $O(1/k^2)$ regime** under Assumption 5.11 with $L_0=0$ (Cor. 5.15) and the result in the nonconvex stochastic setting (Thm. 6.3). This is both **conceptual** (identify a realistic regime for $O(1/k^2)$ with first-order steps + occasional curvature) and **practical** (larger safe steps via HVP gating).
>
>We believe the paper meets both criteria. Empirically, CaCuAdGD consistently outperforms strong non-accelerated baselines and is competitive with accelerated methods on hard instances; theoretically, we provide the standard non-improvable $O(1/k)$ guarantees and a proved local/global $O(1/k^2)$ regime (global under Assumption 5.11 with $L_0=0$). The absence of an accelerated variant does not diminish these results. Accordingly, the **rejection rating does not reflect the paper’s contributions**; we respectfully **request a score reconsideration**.



>**I agree that this paper probably contains interesting insights that bring potential for future research. However, its current presentation is not there yet. I believe the paper still requires a major revision before meeting the publication standard of ICLR.**
>We thank the reviews for pointing out the presentation issues. However, no technical flaws were identified. Moreover, it is explicitly noted that  the paper “probably contains interesting insights with potential for future research. We will apply the clarity edits. In view of this, **we respectfully request a score reconsideration**.

Thank you for the response. Below, I detail my comments.

1. $O(1/K^2)$ rate

   - **Section 5.1**. Although no theorem is stated in **Section 5.1**, the whole section 5.1 (especially the conclusion on line 267) relies on the condition (10), which is essentially an assumption. Otherwise, the $O(1/K^2)$ rate could be misleading to the readers. I would suggest you make these implicit assumptions clear. You might also consider formalizing (10) using assumptions similar to those presented in [1].
   - By "assumptions on the trajectory", I refer to the statement like **Lemma 5.6** and **Corollary 5.7**, where the $O(1/K^2)$ rate only holds for points such that $f(x) - f(x^\star) \geq \big[\frac{3}{2}\frac{L D^2}{\sqrt{H D^3}}\big]^2$. It suggests the acceleration effect stops at some constant accuracy. Morever, this result is counterintuitive: imagine you are optimizing a simple convex quadratic function, then $H = 0$, and the conditions in **Lemma 5.6** and **Corollary 5.7** won't hold since the RHS of the condition $\frac{3}{2}\frac{L D^2}{\sqrt{H D^3}}$ goes to $+\infty$. I don't think this kind of convergence result is acceptable, since it suggests the algorithm performs worse on easier functions.

2. Smoothness terminology

   To my knowledge, in the optimization literature [2], when one says $f$ is $L$-smooth, then it means $f$ has Lipschitz continuous gradient. Similarly, when you say $\nabla f$ is smooth, then $\nabla^2 f$ is Lipschitz continuous. So when you say Hessian smoothness, you are discussing continuity of $\nabla^3 f $. Here, precisely, I believe the algorithm is estimating the smoothness of $f$ along the gradient direction.

3. Incomplete convergence result

   I believe it's better to write down the final convergence rate (complexity), instead of leaving a recursive relation to the readers as in **Theorem 6.3**. Please be precise.

4. Experiments

   I appreciate your honesty about the experiments. But it does not address my concerns: a new algorithm should satisfy at least one of 1) practical efficiency; 2) strong theoretical performance, to be of interest. Given the current theoretical results and experiments, I still don't think they are satisfactory with respect to either criterion.

I agree that this paper probably contains interesting insights that bring potential for future research. However, its current presentation is not there yet. I believe the paper still requires a major revision before meeting the publication standard of ICLR.

**References.**

[1] Fox, C., Mishkin, A., Vaswani, S., & Schmidt, M. (2025). Glocal Smoothness: Line Search can really help!. *arXiv preprint arXiv:2506.12648*.

[2] Nesterov, Y. (2018). *Lectures on convex optimization* (Vol. 137). Berlin: Springer International Publishing.

summary.value:
This paper presents **CaCuTe**, a family of algorithms that leverage **cubic regularization ideas** while avoiding the heavy cost of full cubic‐model solves.  
Starting from the **Lipschitz–Hessian (2H–smooth)** assumption used in classical cubic‐regularized Newton (CRN) methods, the authors derive a **Hessian–vector–based condition** that certifies when a **simple gradient step** will achieve the same decrease as a cubic step.  
This leads to the **CaCuN algorithm**, which dynamically switches between a cheap gradient step and a standard CRN step depending on the local curvature.  
The approach extends to an **accelerated variant (AccCaCuN)** that retains the accelerated \(O(k^{-3})\) global rate, as well as a **first-order adaptive method (CaCuAdGD)** that uses Hessian–vector products and backtracking to adapt \(M_k\) without explicit Hessians.  
A **stochastic version (CaCuSGD)** further generalizes the idea to noisy gradients.  
Overall, the paper provides a unified view of cubic-model techniques that reduce computational cost while maintaining theoretical guarantees.

strengths.value:
- **Clear motivation:** Classical CRN guarantees are strong but expensive; CaCuTe identifies when cheaper first-order steps suffice.  
- **Theoretical soundness:** The paper rigorously derives one-step decrease bounds, global \(O(k^{-2})\) and accelerated \(O(k^{-3})\) rates, and expected stochastic analogues.  
- **Low overhead:** The curvature certificate requires only **one Hessian–vector product**, a modest cost compared to full second-order solves.  
- **Comprehensive framework:** Covers deterministic, accelerated, adaptive, and stochastic regimes under a single analytic template.  
- **Practical relevance:** Algorithms can exploit automatic-differentiation HVPs available in modern ML libraries.

weaknesses.value:
- **Complex exposition:** The notation is dense and the main ideas are sometimes buried in algebraic detail; a higher-level intuition for why the curvature test works would help readers.  
- **Dependence on convexity:** The theoretical results assume convex objectives; it is unclear how the approach behaves on **non-convex** losses where Hessians may be indefinite.  
- **Parameter sensitivity:** The constants used in the curvature condition (e.g., the choice of \(H\) and \(\alpha\)) could affect practical performance, but this dependence is not discussed.    
- **Weak CaCuSGD results:** The empirical performance of **CaCuSGD** appears weak compared to standard **SGD**. It would be interesting to see whether adding **momentum or variance reduction** could mitigate stochastic noise.  
- **Reliance on differing assumptions:** The analysis invokes different assumptions (e.g., Eq. (10), Eq. (14)), making it difficult to compare results across variants. A **summary table** of assumptions and corresponding guarantees would greatly clarify the contributions.  
- **Quantification missing:** The paper does not quantify **how often the full cubic Newton step is avoided** in practice. Reporting this ratio would concretely demonstrate the computational advantage claimed.

questions.value:
1. Could the same idea extend to **non-convex** settings?  
2. In practice, how often does CaCuN actually switch to the cubic step versus taking the cheaper gradient step?  
3. What is the **computational overhead** of the backtracking procedure in CaCuAdGD relative to standard gradient descent?

summary.value:
This paper considered unconstrained minimization problem $\min f(x)$ where $f$ is twice-differentiable and the Hession of $f$ is $2H$-Liptchitz. The paper studies first-order methods in the form of 
$$
x^{k+1} = x^k - \frac{1}{\sqrt{H\|\nabla f(x^k)\|}} \nabla f(x^k).
$$
Combining with cubic regularized Newton steps, the casual cubic Newton method and its acclerated version are proposed. With specific pamameter choices, the casual cubic Newton method recovered the results of the cubic regularized Newton methods. Then under assumptions on bounded Hession eigenvalue in the graident direction, the paper poposed the casual cubic adaptive gradient descent method and extend to directional $L_0, L_1$- smoothness cases. Finally, a variant of methods under stochastic regime is studied.

strengths.value: The paper showed a potential framework to analyze cubid regularized Newton methods and gradient methods under various smoothness regimes.

weaknesses.value: While the core idea presented in this manuscript is interesting and has potential, the current presentation significantly limits its impact. The contribution of the work is not clearly articulated, and the results are not framed with the necessary rigor to be fully convincing. As a result, the contribution of the work remains unclear; see questions below regrading writing, paper structure and the correctness.

comment.value:
The review’s central claims (“unclear contribution,” “insufficient rigor”) are **not supported by any concrete evidence**:

- The paper’s contributions are clearly itemized in Section 1.3.  
- The review does not identify any incorrect theorem, false assumption, or invalid derivation.  
- All results are formally stated (Thm. 4.1, Thm. 5.8, Cor. 5.15, Thm. 6.3) under explicit assumptions (Secs. 2, 5, 6), with complete proofs in the appendices. The review does not engage with any specific line of these proofs or indicate where the arguments would fail.

Instead, the review largely consists of high-level statements and clarifying questions about basic concepts, which point to issues of understanding and exposition rather than to any lack of rigor in the results. In the absence of specific technical faults, we respectfully submit that a **reject recommendation based on unsubstantiated criticism** should carry limited weight. 

The remaining concerns focus on **clarity/presentation**, not correctness. We **disagreed** that the results were unverifiable as written, but we have rewritten the relevant parts (changes marked in teal in the revised version) so that every step is even easier to follow:

- **Contribution cross-referencing.** Each stated contribution now points to the section where it is developed and cross-references the appendix where its proof is located.  
- **Standard assumptions.** Concepts like $L$-smoothness, Hessian–Lipschitz continuity, convexity, and bounded level sets are standard and were **already** cited; we now place the citations **immediately under the assumptions**.  
- **Certificate mechanism.** The presentation is simplified: we either explicitly check the descent inequality or use the step-size rule that implies it.  
- **CaCuN full proof.** We added a **standalone CaCuN theorem** with a complete, self-contained proof. **As initially explained**, the proof follows Nesterov’s approach; we only add a simple one-line implication from the descent inequality used for the gradient branch.  
- **Minor but explicit clarifications.** We include standalone lemmas showing how the descent inequalities yield the stated rates (previously only referenced). We also clarify that Eq. (10) is **illustrative**, and the formal contribution is **Assumption 5.11**.  
- **Typos.** All noted typos are fixed.

**None of these changes alter any claim.** These edits are **purely expository**; statements, assumptions, and rates are unchanged. We ask that the decision focus on the **technical contributions**, not presentation preferences.

summary.value:
**Summary**

This paper establishes the convergence rate of a special stepsize rule for gradient descent under different settings. The stepsize rule is motivated by the optimality condition of the subproblem arising from the cubic regularized Newton's method. Some experiments validate the efficiency of the proposed method.

strengths.value:
**Strength**

The paper is overall easy to follow.

weaknesses.value:
**Weaknesses**

I have several concerns regarding both the theoretical and practical aspects of the paper.

1. Theoretical complexity

   In terms of the theoretical complexity, while the paper claims $O(1/K^2)$ result is achievable using first-order information, the analysis ends up relying on strong assumptions such as equation (10). In general, the first-order methods developed in the paper only guarantee an $O(1/K)$ convergence rate. I find the result relatively weak since it uses extra operations such as the Hessian vector product. Besides, some results (**Corollary 5.7**) in the paper contain strong assumptions on the trajectory, which I find unacceptable; some results (**Theorem 6.3**) are incomplete and do not give a convergence rate.

2. Practical implementation 

   The proposed algorithm is claimed to be parameter-free. However, in most cases, it still requires knowledge of the Hessian Lipschitz constant $H$. Even the adaptive variant still requires a line-search procedure and introduces an additional hyperparameter $\alpha$. Given that the algorithm essentially adopts the gradient direction, I don't think the algorithm design is justified.

3. Weak experiment evaluation

   The experiments in **Section 7**mseem cherry-picked. The results from the appendix suggest the proposed stepsize typically underperforms standard accelerated gradient descent.

Finally, I noticed a number of typos and notation inconsistencies throughout the paper. Overall, I don't think the paper can be published at ICLR in its current form.

summary.value: The paper proposes a ‘casual cubic Newton’ framework, where the algorithm decides whether to use second-order updates or cheaper normalized gradient updates based on a Hessian-vector-product (HVP) certificate, which allows algorithms inspired by the framework (CaCuN and AccCaCun) to enjoy similar convergence rates with cubic-regularized Newton, yet without forming or factorizing Hessians as often. Moreover, under a specific assumption, it is possible to construct an entirely HVP-based algorithm (CaCuAdGD), where the algorithm adapts to the local geometry via the HVP in the ‘certificate inequality’ and the backtracking of the constant $H$.

We thank the reviewer for the quality and thoroughness; the efforts are truly appreciated. However, we recognize that some parts may not have been understood as intended. For that reason we respectfully disagree with the assertions that our results “are not framed with the necessary rigor” and that “the contribution remains unclear.”

>**While the core idea presented in this manuscript is interesting and has potential, the current presentation significantly limits its impact. The contribution of the work is not clearly articulated, and the results are not framed with the necessary rigor to be fully convincing. As a result, the contribution of the work remains unclear; see questions below regrading writing, paper structure and the correctness.**

The paper clearly itemizes the contributions in Sec. 1.3 (Our Contribution; 6 items), we provide a shortened items below

1. **Certificate for cubic-model decrease.** We introduce an HVP-based certificate that decides when the gradient step  achieves the cubic-model (CRN) decrease. 
2. **CaCuN (Casual Cubic Newton).** Using the certificate, CaCuN can skip second-order work while retaining the global $O(k^{-2})$.
3. **AccCaCuN (Accelerated CaCuN).** The same idea applies to the accelerated variant, retaining the global $O(k^{-3})$ rate while avoiding second-order work when the certificate holds.
4. **CaCuAdGD (Casual Cubic Adaptive GD).** We exploit directional curvature via backtracking (see (14)), requiring only HVPs. When the cubic-model decrease does not apply, the method falls back to the quadratic-model decrease. CaCuAdGD is monotone, parameter-free, and shows strong wall-clock performance compared to \algname{AdGD}.
5. **Gradient-directional smoothness relaxation.** We propose an assumption allowing the Hessian eigenvalue in the gradient direction to grow linearly with the square root of the optimality gap. It enables tighter convergence rates and, in particular, a global cubic-model decrease rate.
6. **CaCuSGD (Casual Cubic SGD).** Under standard stochastic assumptions with minibatch gradients and a batched Hessian-gradient estimator, our analysis recovers either the stochastic cubic-Newton decrease or the standard stochastic decrease under $L$-smoothness, corresponding to gradient-norm decay $O(1/k)$ or $O(k^{-1.5})$.

Formal assumptions appear in Sec. 2 (Assumptions 2.1 to 2.3), Sec. 5 (Assumptions 5.5 and 5.11; note that the directional smoothness in Sec. 5.1 is illustrative and intentionally not formalized as an assumption), and Sec. 6 (Assumption 6.1). The main results are Theorem 4.1, Theorem 5.8, Corollary 5.15, and Theorem 6.3, with complete, self-contained proofs in Appendices B, D, and E. We appreciate the observation that Sec. 4.1 (Casual Cubic Newton) presents counterparts for core inequalities used in the original proof, which may not make the result immediately obvious; despite the brevity, the result is rigorously proved. Summing up, we could not identify any specific theorem, assumption, or step that lacks rigor. We invite the reviewer to point to any concrete issues so that we can address them precisely.
To aid readability, we will (a) add explicit cross-references from each contribution and theorem to its proof in the appendix, and (b) provide a standalone theorem and proof for the result in Sec. 4.1 (Casual Cubic Newton).
Given the above, we believe the critique is not substantiated and ask the reviewer to reconsider the reject recommendation unless concrete issues are identified. Below we address the reviewer’s questions. We are also grateful for the other minor issues and typos identified.



>**What are the convergence results of the adaptive gradient methods in the related work?**
To the best of our knowledge all the non-accelerated methods provide only global $O(k^{-1})$ rate. We believe that our results are the first one providing (a) local $O(k^{-2})$ rate, (b) global $O(k^{-2})$ for the relaxed smoothness (when L_0 = 0). For future works we plan to accelerate CaCuAdGD and obtain local $O(k^{-3})$.

>**The sentences and ambiguous words in Section 1.3 are confusing.**
**The first long sentence in Line 89-91 is difficult to understand. I suggest to separate to several sentences. What does the 'corresponds coincides aligns' in the parenthese mean?**
We missed to proofread this sentence. The right version should have been as follows:
We introduce a Hessian-vector-product-based certificate that determines when the decrease from the gradient step $x^{k+1} = x^k - {\nabla f(x^k)}/{\sqrt{H_k\|\nabla f(x^k)\|}}$ matches the decrease guaranteed by the cubic-regularized Newton (CRN) step, where $H_k$ is a local estimate of the Hessian-Lipschitz constant

summary.value: This paper solves an unconstrained optimization problem with a twice-differentiable function $f$ with Lipschitz Hessian. The goal is to obtain an accelerated $O(k^{-2})$ rate while avoiding Hessian evaluation and inversion. The authors accomplish this either under condition in Eq (10) or $L_0, L_1$ Lipschitzness with $L_0=0$. All the reviewers and the authors agree that Eq. (10) is too restrictive. On the other hand, the latter assumption is also rather restrictive and it's not clear what the improvement is with nonzero $L_0$. Moreover, all the reviewers and myself agree that the exposition needs to be improved. Unfortunately, this is significant for a conference paper because there is no way of checking the final version (unlike a journal submission). As a result, a major revision required for exposition is a valid reason for rejection. Given that there are concerns about the contribution (strength of assumptions for the accelerated rate) and the exposition, I recommend rejection.

reviewer_concerns.value: Some of the reviewers concerns about the exposition are resolved. However, an important concern shared by Reviewer Esyd, Reviewer LXQv and Reviewer soLP is that the accelerated rate requires Eq (10) or some Lipschitzness assumptions which are rather strong. The authors made a good case to highlight their Lipschitz assumption holds for some applications, but they are missing a comparison between their results and their assumption as well as similar results in the literature with their corresponding assumptions. A clear positioning and a clearer exposition are not provided during the review period, hence these important concerns are not addressed completely.

Thank you for the positive evaluation of our work. Several of the listed weaknesses are either already addressed in the paper or stem from visibility/presentation rather than missing content. A few items are matters of emphasis rather than substantive gaps. With these clarifications in place, we respectfully ask the reviewer to reconsider and raise the overall score.

>**Complex exposition**
Our analysis relies on two simple descent inequalities derived in Section 3, in Line 177 we state that one of them corresponds to an $O(k^{-2})$ rate. The higher level intuition is summarized in Section 5.4. Please let us know if further clarification would be helpful.

>**Dependence on convexity**
Thanks for the question! That is indeed a very interesting direction to study, we partially did it for the stochastic setting -- we do not assume convexity. However, in Lines 444-445 we state that telescoping each of these one-step descent inequalities is a challenging task. The same holds also for the deterministic setup. More broadly, convexity often guides practical algorithm design. Recent adaptive methods like D-Adaptation [1] and Prodigy [2] show how convexity-inspired ideas enhance nonconvex optimization.

>**Parameter sensitivity**
Indeed, the choice of $H$ may affect the performance. We experiment with the theoretical value proposed in (Mishchenko, 2023). We also propose adaptive methods and compare them against competitors in Sections C and F.2, which do not require a global value H and adapt to the local curvature. Next, we provide extensive discussion on the choice of alfa in Section 5.4. Please let us know if further clarification would be helpful.

>**Weak CaCuSGD results**
We respectfully disagree with the comment. Our stochastic variant triggers curvature steps only when the test certifies a larger guaranteed decrease; otherwise it falls back to SGD. As discussed below the theorem, each of the resulting inequality solely recovers either convergence of SGD, or stochastic cubic Newton in the nonconvex setting -- gradient norm vanishes either as 1/k or 1/k^1.5. Unfortunately, combining these two bounds seems challenging, but one may expect something in between in practice.
Momentum and variance reduction are interesting directions, but they are outside the main scope of CaCuTu; a thorough investigation  would require separate analysis and is deferred to future work.

>**Reliance on differing assumptions**
Note, that equation (10) intentionally is not wrapped as Assumption – the assumption is non-standard and serves mostly for illustrative purposes since it allows us to simply obtain a global $O(k^{-2})$ rate. But it still motivates us to consider a much more interesting relaxation of the standard smoothness – Assumption 5.11, which covers the standard L-smoothness and allows to state the global $O(k^{-2})$ rate if $L_0=0$. This assumption is realistic since it holds for separable logistic regression loss (Example 5.14).

>**Quantification missing**
Unfortunately, we do not have any theoretical result on “expected” oracle costs. However we can comment on experimental behaviour. CaCuN type methods are good in non adaptive settings, i.e. global $H$ is known. But with the adaptive methods available (see Appendix C), proposed methods do not require second order at first iterates at all. For the further iterations, we noticed that local value $H_k$ considerably changes -- after a successful (high objective value decrease) the $H_k$ dramatically increases. After that a few gradient steps are done to recover let’s say.

[2] Mishchenko, Konstantin, and Aaron Defazio. "Prodigy: An expeditiously adaptive parameter-free learner." arXiv preprint arXiv:2306.06101 (2023).

>**some results (Theorem 6.3) are incomplete and do not give a convergence rate.**
As discussed below Theorem 6.3, each resulting inequality recovers one of two regimes in the nonconvex setting: convergence of SGD or convergence of stochastic cubic Newton; the gradient norm vanishes as $1/k$ or as $1/k^{1.5}$, respectively. By extrapolating from the convex setting, we expect faster local convergence. In practice, our experiments show that the approach occasionally allows larger step sizes that dramatically improve convergence while preserving stability. However, combining these two bounds into a single rate appears challenging and, in our view, does not limit the contribution.

>**The experiments in Section 7mseem cherry-picked. The results from the appendix suggest the proposed stepsize typically underperforms standard accelerated gradient descent.**
The section is intentionally named **Selected experiments**, and we refer to the extended experiments in the first sentence. The comparison with accelerated methods is not appropriate, since they have provably faster rates. However, on severe benchmarks such as covtype, w8a, and ill-conditioned logsumexp, CaCuAdGD outperforms accelerated methods. We respectfully but strongly disagree that there is systematic underperformance. Moreover, CaCuAdGD is non-accelerated, so one can expect even faster convergence for an accelerated variant. Also, HVPs are proposed but can be replaced with vector-Hessian-vector products, which do not require backpropagation and can be computed even faster using forward passes only.
We would like to point out that a fair comparison should first consider **non-accelerated adaptive methods**, such as AdGD or Polyak step sizes. These methods work very well on a variety of problems, adapt to local curvature, and do not incur computational overhead such as backtracking and HVP computations. Nevertheless, CaCuAdGD consistently outperforms these methods, which indicates a considerable contribution and validates the significance of the proposed technique.

>**I don't feel I understand what "casual" in the title means. Does it come from the motivation on line 41**
By “casual” we mean on-demand use of second-order information: the proposed methods avoid second-order work whenever possible and invoke it only when it is expected to help. Since it is difficult to predict a priori when this will be beneficial, the use of second-order computations is irregular (that is, occasional).

>**Except for (AccCaCuN), the algorithms developed in the paper search along the gradient direction. Is there any intuition that the resulting algorithm can outperform vanilla gradient descent?**
Although the search direction is the gradient, curvature information enters through the step size. This allows larger safe steps when curvature is mild and smaller steps when it is high, which can outperform vanilla gradient descent. The formalization is given in Section 3 (CRN-like descent result), and the intuition and comparison are discussed in Section 5.4 (Comparison with AdGD). We are happy to provide further details if helpful.
